extracted.intended_audience: Citizens and voters considering ratification of the proposed U.S. Constitution (readers of the Federalist Papers / the public of New York)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and standards for allocating military, fiscal, and related powers between a national government and its member states to preserve the Union and public safety. Focuses on what powers a federal government must hold, limits that are practicable, and institutional arrangements to avoid tyranny or impotence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energetic government necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity of a Constitution at least equally energetic with the one proposed to the preservation of the Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An energetic national government is required to preserve a large union; weaker systems risk dissolution or the need for separate confederacies. The extent of the country strengthens the argument for a strong central government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of federal government
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal purposes to be answered by union are: the common defense of the members; the preservation of the public peace as well against internal convulsions as external attacks; the regulation of commerce with other nations and between the States; the superintendence of our intercourse, political and commercial, with foreign countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These enumerated objects define the domain of federal authority and determine which powers the Union must possess to discharge its duties effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential authorities for common defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities essential to the common defense: to raise armies; to build and equip fleets; to prescribe rules for the government of both; to direct their operations; to provide for their support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These powers ought to exist without limitation because it is impossible to foresee or define the extent and variety of national exigencies; thus, the means must be coextensive with possible combinations of circumstances and under the direction of national councils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means must be proportioned to ends
rubrics_metrics.description: The MEANS ought to be proportioned to the END; the persons, from whose agency the attainment of any END is expected, ought to possess the MEANS by which it is to be attained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once the federal government is entrusted with a function (e.g., common defense), it must be clothed with all requisite powers to accomplish that function; otherwise the trust cannot be executed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal authority over individuals (not merely states)
rubrics_metrics.description: We must extend the laws of the federal government to the individual citizens of America; discard quotas and requisitions, as impracticable and unjust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation addressed only to states (via quotas/requisitions) is ineffective; direct authority over individuals is necessary to secure uniformity, enforcement, and sufficient resources for national objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: National discretion for formation, direction, support of forces
rubrics_metrics.description: No constitutional shackles can wisely be imposed on the power to which the care of common defense is committed with respect to formation, direction, or support of the national forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempts to fix precise limits on such authority risk rendering the government unable to respond to unforeseen dangers; discretion should reside with the national actors charged with the trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discriminate objects among departments with commensurate powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Discriminate the OBJECTS, as far as it can be done, which shall appertain to the different provinces or departments of power; allowing each the most ample authority for fulfilling the objects committed to its charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powers should be allocated by object so each department has adequate authority to achieve its ends; failing to confer power commensurate to the end is imprudent and risks ineffectual governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central government best suited for public defense
rubrics_metrics.description: The national government — as the centre of information, representative of the whole, responsible for the duty assigned, and with authority throughout the States — is best qualified to make suitable provisions for the public defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of its perspective, responsibility, and reach, the central government can establish uniform plans and concerted measures; devolving such duties to states leads to non-cooperation and inefficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratification must rest on consent of the people
rubrics_metrics.description: The fabric of American empire ought to rest on the solid basis of THE CONSENT OF THE PEOPLE; streams of national power ought to flow immediately from that pure, original fountain of all legitimate authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A national government whose legitimacy derives directly from the people (not merely state legislatures) avoids doctrines (like legislative repeal of ratification) that can destabilize federal authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-year appropriation clause as guard (not prohibition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The clause which forbids the appropriation of money for the support of an army for any longer period than two years is a precaution and a real security against the keeping up of troops without evident necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporal limits on appropriations serve as practical checks; absolute prohibitions on standing forces are uncommon and may be ineffective or impracticable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraints on legislative military discretion are improper/unenforceable
rubrics_metrics.description: Restraints upon the discretion of the legislature in respect to military establishments in time of peace, would be improper to be imposed, and if imposed, from the necessities of society, would be unlikely to be observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prohibitions (e.g., no standing armies in peacetime) are either vague, evadable, or would incapacitate the nation by preventing preparation; such rules conflict with likely necessities and will be broken when urgent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing armies (small) in peacetime may be necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Small standing corps in the pay of the government (garrisons, dock-yard guards, etc.) are often necessary in time of peace for frontier defense, protection of arsenals and naval establishments, and to guard against Indian hostilities or foreign encroachments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Militia are impracticable for continuous frontier duties; regular troops maintain readiness, professional skills, and efficiency that militia cannot reliably supply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Militia are insufficient alone for national defense
rubrics_metrics.description: The militia would not long submit to being dragged from their occupations and families; they lack the steadiness and discipline to conduct the steady operations of war against regular and disciplined armies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience in the Revolution shows militia valor but also their limits; economy, stability, and effectiveness generally favor a regular force for sustained operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of leaving defense to individual states
rubrics_metrics.description: Transferring care of the common defense to State governments is an inversion of the primary principle of association and would be oppressive to some States, dangerous to all, and baneful to the Confederacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because dangers (foreign neighbors, frontiers) are common across the Union, defense must be a common responsibility funded and directed by the national government to avoid inequity, free-riding, and dangerous rivalries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perils of separate state military establishments
rubrics_metrics.description: The separate and independent possession of military forces by the States would produce rivalries, mutual jealousies, and a temptation for members to make enterprises upon and subvert the constitutional authority of the Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If several states individually maintain significant forces, other states will seek counterbalances, inflating forces and creating instruments that could be used against national authority; national control helps prevent this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional restrictions that cannot be observed weaken authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Parchment provisions and rules which run counter to the necessities of society are likely to be broken in emergency; every breach of fundamental laws, though dictated by necessity, impairs reverence for the constitution and forms a precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid embedding formal restrictions that are impracticable, because their violation in necessity undermines constitutional stability and invites further breaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid concentrating all important prerogatives in a single assembly
rubrics_metrics.description: Entrusting additional powers to a single assembly (as currently constituted) risks that, by successive augmentations of force, all the most important prerogatives of sovereignty may be accumulated in a single body, producing tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional design should prevent slow accretion of sovereign powers into a single institution by providing appropriate distribution and structure of authority.
